speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: asked the Minister for Education for each of the six local autonomous universities (AUs) (a) what is the size of their endowment fund in each of the past five years; (b) what is the current amount of funds and reserves accumulated; (c) what are the top five uses of these funds; and (d) how much of these funds have been used in each of the past five years.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The size of the endowment funds of our autonomous universities (AUs) is available from their financial reports.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Member also asked for the reserves accumulated.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Reserves are operating surpluses, if any, accumulated over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are typically tied up in assets, which can be buildings, facilities, long-term investments and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The numbers are also available in the financial reports of the AUs, so I will not read them out here.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, what is pertinent is the use of endowment funds.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The AUs set up endowment funds, with Government support, because they should have a separate stream of income such that they can embark on their own programmes and activities without always depending on the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Every year, investments from the endowment fund will generate a return and only a portion of the investment returns is spent, with the rest reinvested.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And this is because the Ministry of Education (MOE) contributes significantly to the endowment funds of the universities, by matching donations that they raise.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The other major uses are providing bursaries and scholarships, supporting additional programmes to enrich students' learning, such as overseas internships and residential learning programmes, funding research projects and sponsoring professorships.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is common practice internationally for universities to build up their endowment funds through donations to support students and activities outside of education, such as research and enterprise.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Donations are always voluntary and decided by donors based on their trust in the organisations and their causes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Donors to AUs will typically specify how the monies are to be used, which AUs do not have the liberty to change.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Can I just seek a couple of clarifications?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It appears that NTU gives out more bursaries and scholarships compared to NUS although NUS has a reserve of $5.9 billion which is more than twice the size of NTU's.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: And SUTD, although it has the least reserve of the three AUs, has more than half of its undergraduates receiving grants for education opportunities and bursaries and scholarships.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: So, can MOE clarify whether there is a discrepancy or is there supposed to be a correlation between the number of bursaries and scholarships given by each AU compared to the reserves they have?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: A second clarification is whether there is a cap that MOE will set for them for the size of endowment fund that the AUs can accumulate over the years?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I do not have the exact numbers and breakdowns to give an analysis.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I am also not sure whether it is factually correct that NTU provides more bursaries than NUS.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We should also take into account that only part of the bursaries and scholarships is funded through the endowment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are also non-endowed donations where donors donate to the university but it is non-endowed, that is, "I donate $100,000.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Please use this $100,000 to distribute and help needy students." Those are non-endowed donations and NUS also has a lot of that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, that assertion I am not sure if it is true.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Compared to international universities, their endowments are not excessively large at all.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, many international universities have endowment funds much bigger than that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Also, more importantly is that the incomes from the endowment funds are put to good use.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: NUS recently put out a statement outlining what they use their money for.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is for research, bursaries and to help with residential programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, I wish to ask the Minister if he thinks that this situation is equitable and whether the Ministry has any policies to try to level the playing field if it is true that the richer universities can give more opportunities to their students than the poorer ones.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, there is some issue of social inequality among the AUs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Just like society, we redistribute wealth, we support the weaker members of society more, but AUs are all not that weak, including our new AUs, such as SIT and SUSS.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The logic is not dissimilar to a society because these are donors who willingly part with their donations to support the universities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They probably saw something they like institutionally and how they use their funds and decide to donate to that particular cause.
